html:
Flux through a patch σk
The teal slab is the fluid that crosses the patch in one unit of time. Drag the slab to slide it along the surface; drag elsewhere to orbit.
Guided demo
⚠ Figure failed to load

elements: curved quadrilateral surface patch σ_k — the teal tile itself, forming the TOP face of the slab, visibly bowed (saddle/dome-like) rather than flat
congruent curved BOTTOM face offset downward along −n, the base of the swept fluid slab
four lofted side walls (front, back, left, right) joining top and bottom faces, translucent teal — this is the volume of fluid crossing in unit time
solid teal outline curves on every visible boundary edge of the slab
dashed teal edges for the two hidden far/back boundary curves
small teal dot marking the sample point (x*_k, y*_k, z*_k) at the center of the bottom curved face
purple/magenta unit normal vector n, long shaft rising from the sample point up through the patch center, topped by a large hollow (outlined, unfilled) triangular arrowhead
bold italic label 'n' just to the right of the arrowhead
exactly two straight black flow arrows pointing upward, one just outside the lower-LEFT outer corner of the slab and one just outside the lower-RIGHT outer corner
label 'Area ΔS_k' at upper right with a single short curved leader arrow touching the top face
label 'σ_k' at left of the slab naming the patch

tan/cream caption callout box with a thick gray border and a thick triangular arrow tail aimed at the slab's lower-right edge, text: 'The volume of fluid crossing σ_k in the direction of n per unit of time.'
live numeric readout: ΔS_k, F·n, and product (F·n)ΔS_k, placed just above the caption box
OPTIONAL (off by default) faint translucent wireframe of the larger host surface from which σ_k was cut

interactions.teaches: The teal solid is not the surface itself but a thin slab of fluid standing on the curved patch; rotating reveals the curved top face, the congruent curved bottom face, and that n is perpendicular to the patch, not vertical in space.

interactions.label: Speed |F|
interactions.teaches: The slab height equals the normal component of F, so the volume crossing σ_k per unit time, (F·n)ΔS_k, grows in direct proportion to the flow speed and collapses to zero when the flow stops.

interactions.label: Angle F to n (°)
interactions.teaches: Only the component of F along n carries fluid through the surface: tilting F toward the tangent plane thins the slab to nothing even though the speed is unchanged, which is why the integrand is a dot product.

interactions.label: Patch area ΔS_k
interactions.teaches: Shrinking the tile shrinks the swept volume proportionally — the second factor in (F·n)ΔS_k — and shows why the flux is built as a Riemann sum over many small patches.
interactions.note: scales the patch's parameter-space footprint about the sample point

interactions.label: Show host surface σ
interactions.teaches: The isolated tile is one cell of a whole surface; revealing the faint host sheet shows that σ_k is a single term of the sum Σ F·n ΔS_k over the entire surface.

interactions.label: Play fluid flow
interactions.teaches: A thin column of fluid rising through the patch and filling exactly the teal slab in one unit of time makes 'volume crossing per unit time' physically concrete.
interactions.note: particles confined to the slab column only — no scattered background particles

demo_steps.title: The patch and its normal
demo_steps.narration: One curved tile σ_k of area ΔS_k is cut from the surface and drawn on its own. The long magenta arrow is the unit normal n erected at the sample point (x*_k, y*_k, z*_k); the teal slab beneath the top face is the fluid that will cross in one unit of time.

demo_steps.title: Faster flow, thicker slab
demo_steps.narration: Raise |F|: the slab grows taller in exact proportion. The volume crossing per unit time is (F·n)ΔS_k, linear in the speed.

demo_steps.title: Tilt F away from n
demo_steps.narration: Keeping the speed fixed but tilting F toward the tangent plane flattens the slab; at 90° the fluid slides along σ_k and nothing crosses. Only F·n counts.

demo_steps.title: Shrink the tile
demo_steps.narration: Make ΔS_k smaller: the swept volume shrinks with the area. Each patch contributes (F·n)ΔS_k, and the flux is the limit of the sum of these contributions.

demo_steps.title: One cell of the whole surface
demo_steps.narration: Reveal the faint host surface: σ_k is just one tile among many. Summing (F·n)ΔS_k over all of them and refining the subdivision gives the flux integral ∬_σ F·n dS.

plan.geometry_notes: FRAMING: the isolated slab must fill ~60–70% of the canvas width. Camera targets the patch center; no host surface visible by default. PATCH: parametrize p(u,v) = (u, v, 0.30 − 0.22u² + 0.16v²) for u∈[−1.1,1.1]·s, v∈[−0.8,0.8]·s where s = patchSize slider (default 1.0). So the default top face spans ~2.2 world units screen-left→right (long axis, receding slightly to upper-left) × ~1.6 units in depth, with a pronounced saddle bow of ±0.25 units — curvature must be clearly visible, not a near-flat plate. SLAB: bottom face = top face translated by −h·n̂(center), thickness h = clamp(|F|·cos(tilt), 0, 3) × 0.35, default ≈0.42, min visible 0.02; even at default the slab should read as a solid tile ~20% as thick as the patch is wide, not a film. NORMAL ARROW: starts at the teal sample dot on the bottom face center, length 1.9 world units (longer than the patch half-width), pointing up and slightly screen-left, tilted with the local surface normal (≈25° off vertical). Hollow outlined triangular arrowhead 0.42 long × 0.30 wide — large and unmistakable. Label 'n' in bold italic 0.2 units right of the head. FLOW ARROWS: exactly TWO, straight, black, vertical on screen, length 1.0, shaft 0.035 thick, solid filled heads; placed 0.35 units outside the lower-LEFT and lower-RIGHT outer corners of the slab base, rising to just past the slab's bottom face. No other arrows, no grey leaders, no free particles. CAPTION: bordered callout occupying the lower-left third of the frame, fill #f7e3b5, 4px border #8a8a8a, black serif text ~18px, with a THICK triangular tail (base ~0.45 of box height) running up-right and touching the slab's lower-right edge. Second small readout line above it: 'ΔS_k = …, F·n = …, (F·n)ΔS_k = …'. LABELS: 'Area ΔS_k' at upper right with one short curved leader to the top face; 'σ_k' italic at the slab's left side, no leader. HOST SURFACE (toggle only): z = 0.30 − 0.22x² + 0.16y² over x∈[−3,3], y∈[−2.2,2.2] as a faint teal wireframe at 20% opacity, drawn behind; camera does not zoom out when enabled. COLORS: patch/slab faces translucent teal #8fdcd0→#c7ece4 at 55% opacity, outline edges #0f9a9a 2px, hidden edges same color dashed; normal arrow #b45fd0 shaft with #d9a8ea highlight, sample dot #0f9a9a; flow arrows #000. MATH: slab height along n = |F|cos(θ); displayed volume = (F·n)·ΔS_k with ΔS_k computed as the numerically integrated area of the parametric top face.
plan.notes: Build top and bottom faces as ParametricBufferGeometry from the same p(u,v), the bottom simply offset by −h·n̂; loft the shared boundary loop into the four side walls so top, bottom and walls stay watertight as sliders change. Compute the true normal at (0,0) via cross(p_u, p_v) each frame and orient the arrow group to it. Use transparent MeshStandardMaterial with depthWrite:false plus a separate LineSegments pass for crisp outlines; hidden back edges via LineDashedMaterial + computeLineDistances(). Draw the hollow arrowhead as an outlined cone (EdgesGeometry on a ConeGeometry with an unfilled/very low-opacity interior) so it matches the source's open triangle. Keep all text as CSS2D/HTML overlays that never rotate with the camera; side-panel slider labels must be short enough to fit one line (use the given short labels and put units in the value readout). Animation: ~40 instanced points confined to the prism between bottom and top face, advected along F, recycled at the top — disable entirely when the animation is off so nothing stray remains on screen.

authoredPrompt: This figure shows a single curved surface patch sigma_k in 3D space, illustrating the geometric meaning of the integrand in the surface flux integral. The patch sigma_k is depicted as a curved tile (teal) with its area labeled Delta_Sk; a unit normal vector n (purple arrow, pointing upward) is drawn at the center of the patch, and black arrows along the sides indicate the direction of fluid flow passing through the surface. A caption box connected to the patch reads: The volume of fluid crossing sigma_k in the direction of n per unit of time. The figure illustrates that the quantity F(x*_k, y*_k, z*_k) dot n(x*_k, y*_k, z*_k) Delta_Sk approximates the volume of fluid passing through the patch in the normal direction per unit time, motivating the Riemann sum definition of the flux integral.

- Drag the surface patch σₖ to different locations on the full surface and watch the outward normal vector n reorient and the patch area ΔSₖ update
- Slider for flow velocity magnitude: show how the volume of fluid crossing the patch in the direction of n per unit time scales proportionally

interactions.teaches: The unit normal n is a local property: sliding the patch across the curved host surface reorients n to stay perpendicular to the surface there, and the patch area ΔS_k changes where the surface is more steeply curved.
The teal solid is not the surface itself but a thin slab of fluid sitting on the patch; rotating shows its curved top, curved bottom, and the normal direction standing off the surface.

interactions.label: Flow speed |F| (normal component)
interactions.teaches: The swept slab height equals F·n, so the volume crossing σ_k per unit time, (F·n)ΔS_k, scales in direct proportion to the flow speed — and vanishes when the flow is zero.

interactions.label: Angle between F and n (degrees)
interactions.teaches: Only the component of F along n carries fluid through the surface: tilting F toward the tangent plane shrinks the slab to zero even though the speed is unchanged.

interactions.label: Play fluid flow
interactions.teaches: Particles streaming upward through the patch make visible what 'volume crossing σ_k per unit time' means physically.

demo_steps.title: The patch and its normal
demo_steps.narration: A small curved tile σ_k of area ΔS_k is cut from the surface, with the unit normal n erected at the sample point. The teal slab above it is the fluid that will cross in one unit of time.

demo_steps.title: Faster flow, bigger volume
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the flow speed thickens the slab proportionally: the volume crossing per unit time is (F·n)ΔS_k, linear in |F|.

demo_steps.title: Tilting the flow
demo_steps.narration: Tilting F away from n keeps the speed the same but shrinks the slab — at 90° the fluid slides along the surface and nothing crosses it.

demo_steps.title: Move the patch
demo_steps.narration: Drag the patch to a new place on the host surface: n swings to the new outward direction and ΔS_k updates, which is why the flux must be summed patch by patch.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Host surface: a gently bowed sheet z = 0.25 - 0.12x² - 0.10y² spanning x∈[-3,3], y∈[-2.5,2.5], drawn as a faint translucent teal wireframe. Patch σ_k: a parameter-space square of side ~2.0 in x and ~1.4 in y centered at the draggable sample point (default near the surface apex, appearing slightly left of frame center and in the upper half of the frame, matching the source). Patch is visibly curved (bows upward toward the viewer's left-rear) with its long axis running screen-left to screen-right and receding to the upper-left. Slab thickness (swept height, measured along n) = |F| cos(tilt) × 0.4 world units, default ≈0.48; thickness 0 when tilt = ±90°. Purple normal arrow: shaft length 1.6 units starting at the teal sample dot on the bottom face and rising through the top face, pointing up and slightly screen-up-left, hollow triangular arrowhead ~0.25 units. Two black flow arrows of length ~0.9 units, vertical on screen, placed just outside the left and right lower corners of the patch. Colors: patch faces translucent teal gradient #9fe0d4 → #cdeee4 at ~55% opacity, patch edges #12a8a8, dashed hidden edges same teal dashed; normal arrow shaft #b878c8 with lighter #d9b3e3 lower half and #12a8a8 base dot; flow arrows black #000; caption box fill #fbe0a8 with 3px gray border #9a9a9a and a leftward pointer tab meeting the patch's lower-right side; label text black serif/italic math. Caption box occupies the lower half of the frame, patch the upper half. Volume per unit time displayed as (F·n)ΔS_k with F·n = |F|cos(tilt).
interactionPlan.notes: Build the patch and slab as parametric BufferGeometry sampled from the host surface function so dragging simply re-evaluates the parametrization; recompute the exact surface normal via cross product of the partial derivatives each frame and orient the purple ArrowHelper-style mesh (custom cone for the hollow-outline arrowhead) to it. Render patch side walls by lofting the patch boundary along n·thickness. Use MeshBasicMaterial/MeshStandardMaterial with transparent:true, depthWrite:false and a separate LineSegments pass for the crisp teal outlines; hidden back edges drawn with LineDashedMaterial and computeLineDistances(). Labels ('n', 'Area ΔS_k', 'Surface σ_k') and the caption box as CSS2D/HTML overlays with SVG curved leader arrows so text stays crisp and unrotated during orbit. Fluid particles: an instanced point cloud advected along the F direction, recycled after passing through the slab, speed tied to the flowSpeed slider. Show a live readout of ΔS_k, F·n, and their product near the caption box.

discrepancies: A large gridded host surface (wireframe sheet) dominates the scene; the source shows only the isolated curved slab. This shrinks the patch to a small fraction of the frame and changes the composition substantially.
The slab is much thinner and flatter than in the source, where the tile is a prominently curved, fairly thick teal solid with strongly visible curved top/bottom faces.
The unit-normal arrow is proportionally short with a very small hollow head; in the source it is a tall, visually dominant magenta arrow roughly as long as the slab is wide.

Extra elements not in the source: animated teal fluid particles and a grey leader arrow connecting the caption, plus what reads as a third black flow arrow near the patch (source shows exactly two black upward arrows at the outer lower corners).
The caption callout box is small and generic compared to the source's large bordered speech-box with a thick pointed arrow tail into the slab.
Overall zoom leaves the figure occupying a small part of the canvas, with large empty margins, making the tile detail (dashed hidden edges, sample dot) hard to read.
evaluation.notes: Conceptually excellent and richly interactive (speed/tilt sliders, draggable patch, guided demo, live flux readout) with correct 3D slab geometry and dashed hidden edges, but the added dominant host-surface grid, thin slab, undersized normal arrow and small overall framing make it noticeably less recognizable as the source figure.

interactions.teaches: The teal solid is not the surface itself but a thin slab of fluid standing on the curved patch; rotating reveals the curved top face, the congruent curved bottom face, and that n is perpendicular to the patch, not vertical in space.

interactions.label: Speed |F|
interactions.teaches: The slab height equals the normal component of F, so the volume crossing σ_k per unit time, (F·n)ΔS_k, grows in direct proportion to the flow speed and collapses to zero when the flow stops.

interactions.label: Angle F to n (°)
interactions.teaches: Only the component of F along n carries fluid through the surface: tilting F toward the tangent plane thins the slab to nothing even though the speed is unchanged, which is why the integrand is a dot product.

interactions.label: Patch area ΔS_k
interactions.teaches: Shrinking the tile shrinks the swept volume proportionally — the second factor in (F·n)ΔS_k — and shows why the flux is built as a Riemann sum over many small patches.
interactions.note: scales the patch's parameter-space footprint about the sample point

interactions.label: Show host surface σ
interactions.teaches: The isolated tile is one cell of a whole surface; revealing the faint host sheet shows that σ_k is a single term of the sum Σ F·n ΔS_k over the entire surface.

interactions.label: Play fluid flow
interactions.teaches: A thin column of fluid rising through the patch and filling exactly the teal slab in one unit of time makes 'volume crossing per unit time' physically concrete.
interactions.note: particles confined to the slab column only — no scattered background particles

demo_steps.title: The patch and its normal
demo_steps.narration: One curved tile σ_k of area ΔS_k is cut from the surface and drawn on its own. The long magenta arrow is the unit normal n erected at the sample point (x*_k, y*_k, z*_k); the teal slab beneath the top face is the fluid that will cross in one unit of time.

demo_steps.title: Faster flow, thicker slab
demo_steps.narration: Raise |F|: the slab grows taller in exact proportion. The volume crossing per unit time is (F·n)ΔS_k, linear in the speed.

demo_steps.title: Tilt F away from n
demo_steps.narration: Keeping the speed fixed but tilting F toward the tangent plane flattens the slab; at 90° the fluid slides along σ_k and nothing crosses. Only F·n counts.

demo_steps.title: Shrink the tile
demo_steps.narration: Make ΔS_k smaller: the swept volume shrinks with the area. Each patch contributes (F·n)ΔS_k, and the flux is the limit of the sum of these contributions.

demo_steps.title: One cell of the whole surface
demo_steps.narration: Reveal the faint host surface: σ_k is just one tile among many. Summing (F·n)ΔS_k over all of them and refining the subdivision gives the flux integral ∬_σ F·n dS.

plan.geometry_notes: FRAMING: the isolated slab must fill ~60–70% of the canvas width. Camera targets the patch center; no host surface visible by default. PATCH: parametrize p(u,v) = (u, v, 0.30 − 0.22u² + 0.16v²) for u∈[−1.1,1.1]·s, v∈[−0.8,0.8]·s where s = patchSize slider (default 1.0). So the default top face spans ~2.2 world units screen-left→right (long axis, receding slightly to upper-left) × ~1.6 units in depth, with a pronounced saddle bow of ±0.25 units — curvature must be clearly visible, not a near-flat plate. SLAB: bottom face = top face translated by −h·n̂(center), thickness h = clamp(|F|·cos(tilt), 0, 3) × 0.35, default ≈0.42, min visible 0.02; even at default the slab should read as a solid tile ~20% as thick as the patch is wide, not a film. NORMAL ARROW: starts at the teal sample dot on the bottom face center, length 1.9 world units (longer than the patch half-width), pointing up and slightly screen-left, tilted with the local surface normal (≈25° off vertical). Hollow outlined triangular arrowhead 0.42 long × 0.30 wide — large and unmistakable. Label 'n' in bold italic 0.2 units right of the head. FLOW ARROWS: exactly TWO, straight, black, vertical on screen, length 1.0, shaft 0.035 thick, solid filled heads; placed 0.35 units outside the lower-LEFT and lower-RIGHT outer corners of the slab base, rising to just past the slab's bottom face. No other arrows, no grey leaders, no free particles. CAPTION: bordered callout occupying the lower-left third of the frame, fill #f7e3b5, 4px border #8a8a8a, black serif text ~18px, with a THICK triangular tail (base ~0.45 of box height) running up-right and touching the slab's lower-right edge. Second small readout line above it: 'ΔS_k = …, F·n = …, (F·n)ΔS_k = …'. LABELS: 'Area ΔS_k' at upper right with one short curved leader to the top face; 'σ_k' italic at the slab's left side, no leader. HOST SURFACE (toggle only): z = 0.30 − 0.22x² + 0.16y² over x∈[−3,3], y∈[−2.2,2.2] as a faint teal wireframe at 20% opacity, drawn behind; camera does not zoom out when enabled. COLORS: patch/slab faces translucent teal #8fdcd0→#c7ece4 at 55% opacity, outline edges #0f9a9a 2px, hidden edges same color dashed; normal arrow #b45fd0 shaft with #d9a8ea highlight, sample dot #0f9a9a; flow arrows #000. MATH: slab height along n = |F|cos(θ); displayed volume = (F·n)·ΔS_k with ΔS_k computed as the numerically integrated area of the parametric top face.
